title: Lee's despair and the Chicago state institution ordeal
summary: Lee, unhappy he could not blow, overdosed and was sent to a state institution where he was beaten; Mary walked him out and took him to hospital.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Well, he really, when he was in the hospitals and things, he was very unhappy because he always had hopes of blowing his trumpet again. He was despondent to what extent, once, that he took about 20 Nevitol. And we went to the hospital. I got back home in time to get him in the hospital. And he really, he always said he didn't want to live if he couldn't blow. But I always tried to encourage him and tell him that he would blow again. And that's what his doctors insist on me doing. Because his... He needed some hope to... Right. He had to have it. And one incident that happened to him, and to this day, I mention it every time I get an opportunity to do so. Chicago have a system there that people that attempt suicide or they think they are something, they have a habit of sending them to a state institution for, you know, psych treatments. Well, he was sent out there to be friends. A judge determines what's to be done. Right. So, a friend of his and I were out there that day and we carried his clothes thinking we were bringing back home. And this judge said, no, he couldn't be brought back. He'd have to go and take these treatments. Well, he was very ill at the time. He'd had pneumonia also. Mm-hmm. So, they did send him out there. Well, I used to go see him and he said, oh, when he first sent him out there, they put drunks and whatnot mixed up with patients that shouldn't be. Yeah. And as soon as he got in, they told him to mop or do something, but anyway, they beat him up. And when I got out and found out he was beating up, I insisted they put him in the hospital after I got out there. So, they would not release him to me. I had to get a lawyer. So, I got a lawyer and this lawyer looked like to me he was not going to get him out there. I went to the superintendent, but not released him. So, I decided on doing this. He could walk on the grounds. I said, look, they're not letting you out of here and you've got to have treatment. Come on, let's go. But we both, I was so frightened because you know you're not supposed to do that. Yeah. Thank you. So, I walked him out the gate. You saw? And we took buses and streetcars every direction because I didn't want them because they would have probably, you know, arrested me for taking him. And I took him home. Then I took him to the hospital. And so, I called up the superintendent and told him that I had him in the hospital. And so, he said, well, come out and we want to straighten this out. And they got frightened after that. Yeah. So, they wanted me to come out and sign the papers that, you know, they released him. But I refused to do it. So, then they wrote me letters and letters to come. But I still would not go. And that was when Lee stayed in the hospital for quite a long time.
